knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as a composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{tan}⁡u,\,u=1{x}^{4}-17.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\sec^{2}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4{x}^{3}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\sec^{2}⁡u\cdot 4{x}^{3} \\  & =4{x}^{3}\sec^{2}⁡u \\  & =4{x}^{3}\sec^{2}⁡(1{x}^{4}-17).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
y=\operatorname{tan}⁡u,\,u=7{x}^{4}-6.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\sec^{2}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=28{x}^{3}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\sec^{2}⁡u\cdot 28{x}^{3} \\  & =28{x}^{3}\sec^{2}⁡u \\  & =28{x}^{3}\sec^{2}⁡(7{x}^{4}-6).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as a composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{tan}⁡u,\,u=8{x}^{4}-6.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\sec^{2}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=32{x}^{3}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\sec^{2}⁡u\cdot 32{x}^{3} \\  & =32{x}^{3}\sec^{2}⁡u \\  & =32{x}^{3}\sec^{2}⁡(8{x}^{4}-6).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express $y$ as a composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{tan}⁡u,\,u=16{x}^{4}-1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\sec^{2}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=64{x}^{3}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\sec^{2}⁡u\cdot 64{x}^{3} \\  & =64{x}^{3}\sec^{2}⁡u \\  & =64{x}^{3}\sec^{2}⁡(16{x}^{4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u=1x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡u)\cdot 1 \\  & =1\operatorname{cos}⁡(1x).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =1\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =1\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =1\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is 

$$
m={f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{58}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{58}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u=29x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=29.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡u)\cdot 29 \\  & =29\operatorname{cos}⁡(29x).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{58},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{58}) & =29\operatorname{cos}⁡(29\cdot \frac{\pi }{58}) \\  & =29\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =29\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{58}$ is 

$$
m={f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{58})=0.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x=1$ is given by $f'(1).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y = \sin{u}, \qquad u = \pi \left(x^{2} +1x - 2\right).
$$

Differentiating gives
$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \pi (2x + 1).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get


$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\

&=\cos u \cdot \pi (2x+1)\\

&=\pi (2x+1)\cos u\\

&=\pi (2x+1)\cos \left(  \pi \left(x^{2} +1x - 2\right) \right).
\end{aligned}
$$


Evaluating at $x=1,$ we find


$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(1) & =\pi (2\cdot1+1)\cos \left(  \pi \left(1^{2} +1\cdot1 - 2\right) \right) \\

& =3\pi \cos(0\pi) \\
&= 3\pi \cdot (1) \\
&= 3\pi
\end{aligned}
$$


Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 1$ is 
$$
m = f'(1) = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{3\pi}.
$$

The slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x=1$ is given by $f'(1).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y = \sin{u}, \qquad u = \pi \left(x^{2} +7x - 2\right).
$$

Differentiating gives
$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \pi (2x + 7).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get


$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\

&=\cos u \cdot \pi (2x+7)\\

&=\pi (2x+7)\cos u\\

&=\pi (2x+7)\cos \left(  \pi \left(x^{2} +7x - 2\right) \right).
\end{aligned}
$$


Evaluating at $x=1,$ we find


$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(1) & =\pi (2\cdot1+7)\cos \left(  \pi \left(1^{2} +7\cdot1 - 2\right) \right) \\

& =9\pi \cos(6\pi) \\
&= 9\pi \cdot (1) \\
&= 9\pi
\end{aligned}
$$


Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 1$ is 
$$
m = f'(1) = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{9\pi}.
$$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y = \sin{u}, \qquad u = \pi \left(x^{2} +24x - 2\right).
$$

Differentiating gives
$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \pi (2x + 24).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get


$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\

&=\cos u \cdot \pi (2x+24)\\

&=\pi (2x+24)\cos u\\

&=\pi (2x+24)\cos \left(  \pi \left(x^{2} +24x - 2\right) \right).
\end{aligned}
$$


Evaluating at $x=1,$ we find


$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(1) & =\pi (2\cdot1+24)\cos \left(  \pi \left(1^{2} +24\cdot1 - 2\right) \right) \\

& =26\pi \cos(23\pi) \\
&= 26\pi \cdot (-1) \\
&= -26\pi
\end{aligned}
$$


Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 1$ is 
$$
m = f'(1) = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-26\pi}.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x=1$ is given by $f'(1).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y = \sin{u}, \qquad u = \pi \left(2x^{2} +17x - 2\right).
$$

Differentiating gives
$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \pi (4x + 17).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get


$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\

&=\cos u \cdot \pi (4x+17)\\

&=\pi (4x+17)\cos u\\

&=\pi (4x+17)\cos \left(  \pi \left(2x^{2} +17x - 2\right) \right).
\end{aligned}
$$


Evaluating at $x=1,$ we find


$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(1) & =\pi (4\cdot1+17)\cos \left(  \pi \left(2\cdot1^{2} +17\cdot1 - 2\right) \right) \\

& =21\pi \cos(17\pi) \\
&= 21\pi \cdot (-1) \\
&= -21\pi
\end{aligned}
$$


Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 1$ is 
$$
m = f'(1) = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-21\pi}.
$$

The slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x=1$ is given by $f'(1).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y = \sin{u}, \qquad u = \pi \left(10x^{2} +11x - 2\right).
$$

Differentiating gives
$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \pi (20x + 11).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get


$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\

&=\cos u \cdot \pi (20x+11)\\

&=\pi (20x+11)\cos u\\

&=\pi (20x+11)\cos \left(  \pi \left(10x^{2} +11x - 2\right) \right).
\end{aligned}
$$


Evaluating at $x=1,$ we find


$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(1) & =\pi (20\cdot1+11)\cos \left(  \pi \left(10\cdot1^{2} +11\cdot1 - 2\right) \right) \\

& =31\pi \cos(19\pi) \\
&= 31\pi \cdot (-1) \\
&= -31\pi
\end{aligned}
$$


Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 1$ is 
$$
m = f'(1) = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-31\pi}.
$$

The slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x=1$ is given by $f'(1).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y = \sin{u}, \qquad u = \pi \left(18x^{2} +5x - 2\right).
$$

Differentiating gives
$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \pi (36x + 5).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get


$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\

&=\cos u \cdot \pi (36x+5)\\

&=\pi (36x+5)\cos u\\

&=\pi (36x+5)\cos \left(  \pi \left(18x^{2} +5x - 2\right) \right).
\end{aligned}
$$


Evaluating at $x=1,$ we find


$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(1) & =\pi (36\cdot1+5)\cos \left(  \pi \left(18\cdot1^{2} +5\cdot1 - 2\right) \right) \\

& =41\pi \cos(21\pi) \\
&= 41\pi \cdot (-1) \\
&= -41\pi
\end{aligned}
$$


Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 1$ is 
$$
m = f'(1) = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-41\pi}.
$$

We will calculate ${f}^{'}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}u,\,u={x}^{2}+1x-16.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x+1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}u\cdot (2x+1) \\  & =(2x+1)\operatorname{cos}u \\  & =(2x+1)\operatorname{cos}({x}^{2}+1x-16).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(0) & =(2\cdot 0+1)\operatorname{cos}({0}^{2}+1\cdot 0-16) \\  & =1\operatorname{cos}(-16) \\  & =1\operatorname{cos}16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is $1\operatorname{cos}16.$

We will calculate ${f}^{'}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}u,\,u={x}^{2}+1x-10.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x+1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}u\cdot (2x+1) \\  & =(2x+1)\operatorname{cos}u \\  & =(2x+1)\operatorname{cos}({x}^{2}+1x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(0) & =(2\cdot 0+1)\operatorname{cos}({0}^{2}+1\cdot 0-10) \\  & =1\operatorname{cos}(-10) \\  & =1\operatorname{cos}10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is $1\operatorname{cos}10.$

The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is given by ${f}^{'}(0).$

We will calculate ${f}^{'}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}u,\,u={x}^{2}+8x-3.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x+8.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}u\cdot (2x+8) \\  & =(2x+8)\operatorname{cos}u \\  & =(2x+8)\operatorname{cos}({x}^{2}+8x-3).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(0) & =(2\cdot 0+8)\operatorname{cos}({0}^{2}+8\cdot 0-3) \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}(-3) \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is $8\operatorname{cos}3.$

The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is given by ${f}^{'}(0).$

We will calculate ${f}^{'}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}u,\,u={x}^{2}+16x-12.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x+16.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}u\cdot (2x+16) \\  & =(2x+16)\operatorname{cos}u \\  & =(2x+16)\operatorname{cos}({x}^{2}+16x-12).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(0) & =(2\cdot 0+16)\operatorname{cos}({0}^{2}+16\cdot 0-12) \\  & =16\operatorname{cos}(-12) \\  & =16\operatorname{cos}12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is $16\operatorname{cos}12.$

The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is given by ${f}^{'}(0).$

We will calculate ${f}^{'}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}u,\,u={x}^{2}+23x-5.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x+23.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}u\cdot (2x+23) \\  & =(2x+23)\operatorname{cos}u \\  & =(2x+23)\operatorname{cos}({x}^{2}+23x-5).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(0) & =(2\cdot 0+23)\operatorname{cos}({0}^{2}+23\cdot 0-5) \\  & =23\operatorname{cos}(-5) \\  & =23\operatorname{cos}5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is $23\operatorname{cos}5.$

We will calculate ${f}^{'}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x+24.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}u\cdot (2x+24) \\  & =(2x+24)\operatorname{cos}u \\  & =(2x+24)\operatorname{cos}({x}^{2}+24x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(0) & =(2\cdot 0+24)\operatorname{cos}({0}^{2}+24\cdot 0-1) \\  & =24\operatorname{cos}(-1) \\  & =24\operatorname{cos}1\end{aligned}
